Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn representations by predicting the embedding of one part of an input from the embedding of another part, with no negative examples and no reconstruction loss. They are prone to representation collapse, in which the learned embeddings degenerate to a constant or to very low rank. In practice collapse is avoided with a collection of empirical heuristics (how the predictor is designed and scaled, how much of the input is masked, how the target encoder is updated), and no single account explains why they work. The insight to build on: collapse is decided early in training, near the collapsed solution, where two effects compete in every direction of representation space, a driving force that grows the direction and a decay effect that shrinks it. Whether a direction survives, and therefore how much rank the representation can develop, depends on which of the two is stronger there. The research problem is to turn this insight into a theory that explains and predicts when JEPAs collapse and what the common heuristics change, and to test that theory empirically.
